questions.question: 8. Patient presents with cough, stridor, and dyspnea. On examination, there was lymphadenopathy. Histopathological examination of the lymph node shows granulomas with giant cells and stellate concretions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease that most commonly presents as cough, dyspnea, dry eyes, and usually has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Lesions of the eyes and skin are also very common in these patients. It is seen more in middle-aged women than in men. Sarcoidosis results from an increase in CD4+ T-cells (increased CD4+:CD8+ ratio). As a result, cytokines like IL-2, TNF, IL-8, and IFN-gamma will increase. These cytokines are the cause of granuloma formation in this disorder. It presents with granulomas in multiple organs. They are classically described as non-caseating granulomas composed of epithelioid macrophages with giant cells. There is no central necrosis as there would be in tubercular granulomas. Naked granulomas are non-caseating granulomas minimally surrounded by lymphocytes. Star-shaped inclusions called asteroid bodies (stellate concretions) and laminated calcium and protein-containing bodies called Schaumann bodies are also found in the giant cells of most of these granulomas. These are not pathognomonic to sarcoidosis and can also be found in other granulomatous diseases like tuberculosis.



Other options: Option A: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) occurs due to inhalational exposure to a number of antigens, causing inflammation of the alveoli and the small airways. The cause of the inflammation is dysregulated Th1 and Th17 immune response (type IV hypersensitivity). Lung biopsy shows the formation of noncaseating granulomas, but they are poorly defined. Option B: Churg-Strauss syndrome (Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis) involves the skin, cardiac and gastrointestinal tract, and peripheral nervous system with associated eosinophilia. Biopsy shows necrotizing vasculitis with eosinophilic infiltrates and eosinophilic granulomas. Option C: Tuberculosis has more constitutional symptoms with granulomas showing caseous necrosis, abundant lymphocytes, and acid-fast bacilli. Pearl PM2355: Types of granulomas

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: 9. Caspases are involved in which of the following types of programmed cell death?
questions.explanation:
Caspases are involved in Pyroptosis and Apoptosis. Pyroptosis is a form of cell death driven by the release of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1. When cytoplasmic innate immune receptors detect microbial components inside cells, they trigger the formation of a multiprotein complex called the inflammasome. The inflammasome activates caspase-1, which in turn promotes the release of active IL-1. Caspases 4 and 5 can also contribute to this cell death. Unlike apoptosis, pyroptosis is marked by the release of inflammatory molecules. Apoptosis involves both intrinsic (mitochondrial) and extrinsic (death receptor) pathways, which converge to activate a caspase cascade. The caspases involved in apoptosis include initiator caspases (8, 9 & 10) and executioner caspases (3, 6, & 7). The following image depicts the apoptotic pathway:

Necroptosis is a caspase-independent, programmed form of necrosis. It combines features of necrosis (ATP depletion, swelling, membrane rupture) with programmed regulation. It involves two kinases called receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 and 3 (RIPK1 and RIPK3) Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent pathway driven by lipid peroxidation. This disrupts membrane integrity and leads to cell death resembling necrosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: 10. A child presented with fatigue, jaundice, and splenomegaly. His father also has had a similar history. On peripheral smear, MCHC was found to be elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical features, along with an increased MCHC (mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration) and a family history, are suggestive of hereditary spherocytosis.  Hereditary spherocytosis is a type of hereditary hemolytic anemia that is passed down in an autosomal dominant pattern. Mutations of the red blood cell surface proteins spectrin and ankyrin can result in unstable cell membranes, leading to hemolysis. This disorder can present at a young age with severe jaundice and fatigue. The unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia predisposes the patient to develop gallstones. Hence, childhood gallstones should raise suspicion for this diagnosis. The laboratory findings include normocytic anemia with unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is usually normal or slightly decreased, the mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) is characteristically increased (>34 g/dL), and hematocrit is decreased due to hemolytic anemia. The peripheral smear will show large spherical red blood cells without central pallor (shown in the image below). Osmotic fragility test, acid glycerol lysis test and the eosin-5′-maleimide (EMA)–binding test help in diagnosing hereditary spherocytosis. There is no specific treatment available besides splenectomy. However, due to the possible adverse effects, it is only indicated in severe cases and after the child attains puberty in moderate cases. It should be followed up with the appropriate antibiotic and vaccine prophylaxis.

Other options: Option A: Thalassemia is a hereditary hemoglobinopathy resulting from deficient synthesis of one or more globin chains. It is associated with microcytic hypochromic anemia (low MCHC), typically with low MCV and MCH. Option B: Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a point mutation in the β-globin gene, replacing glutamic acid with valine. This leads to polymerization of deoxygenated HbS and the formation of sickle-shaped RBCs. Option D: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) is due to antibody and complement-mediated destruction of RBCs. Diagnosis is confirmed using the Coombs test. The direct Coombs test detects antibodies bound to RBCs, while the indirect test identifies antibodies in the serum. questions.question: 11. A 60-year-old man presents with weakness, fatigue, and bleeding tendencies. His peripheral smear showed 25% blast-like cells, as shown in the image. What is the most common type of genetic abnormality seen in this hematological malignancy?
questions.explanation:
A peripheral blood smear revealing 25% blast-like cells along with prominent faggot cells (blast cells containing multiple Auer rods) strongly points towards acute myeloid leukemia (AML) subtype M3, also known as acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). The most common genetic association with this leukemia is t(15;17), resulting in a PML-RARA fusion gene. Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a malignancy of hematopoietic progenitor cells with impaired differentiation, causing accumulation of immature myeloid blasts in the bone marrow. This replacement of normal blast cells in the marrow leads to anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia, along with their associated clinical manifestations. Anemia causes weakness and fatigue, thrombocytopenia increases bleeding tendencies, and neutropenia predisposes to fever and infections. In AML-M3, the malignant cells release large quantities of procoagulants and fibrinolytic factors that can cause disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and further increase the bleeding tendency. This subtype of AML can be treated with targeted therapy that uses all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic salts. They have the best prognosis among different subtypes of AML and a high cure rate. The following image demonstrates typical myeloblasts containing Auer rods as seen in acute myeloid leukemia.

Other options: Option A: inv(16) or inversion 16 is typically observed in acute myelomonocytic leukemia (AML-M4). Option B: t(8;21) is characteristic of AML with maturation (AML-M2). Option C: AML with NPM1 is recognized as a distinct entity per the WHO classification that shows normal cytogenetics with the NPM1 gene mutation. Pearl PM1998: Important Translocations in AML

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: 12. A 6-month-old infant presents with recurrent infections and failure to thrive. Laboratory investigations reveal decreased B cells, T cells, and a deficiency of adenosine deaminase (ADA). Which of the following immunodeficiency disorders is most likely associated?
questions.explanation:
Recurrent infections, failure to thrive, decreased B-cell and T-cells, along with the deficiency of adenosine deaminase (ADA), are suggestive of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). SCID affects both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses, primarily impacting T cells and resulting in the absence or severe underdevelopment of lymphoid tissues like lymph nodes and tonsils. The thymus biopsy shows remnants of Hassall's corpuscles.  Affected children present with prominent thrush (oral candidiasis), extensive diaper rash, and failure to thrive. Some patients develop a morbilliform rash shortly after birth because maternal T cells are transferred across the placenta and attack the fetus, causing graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). Persons with SCID are extremely susceptible to recurrent, severe infections by a wide range of pathogens, including:  * Candida albicans * Pneumocystis jiroveci * Pseudomonas * Cytomegalovirus * Varicella There are two main types of SCID: * X-linked SCID: The most common form, caused by a mutation in the common γ-chain (γc) subunit of cytokine receptors. This leads to reduced T-cell numbers and impaired antibody synthesis despite normal B-cell counts. The thymus shows undifferentiated epithelial cells. * Autosomal recessive SCID: Often due to ADA deficiency, causing toxic metabolite accumulation that damages T cells, resulting in greater T-cell reduction. Other, less common autosomal recessive causes of SCID involve RAG and JAK3 mutations. In both forms, the thymus is small and lacks lymphoid cells, but ADA deficiency uniquely features remnants of Hassall’s corpuscles. Other options:  Option A: Hypogammaglobulinemia is characterized by reduced immunoglobulin levels, affecting humoral immunity. Transient hypogammaglobulinemia can occur in children under 6 months of age and is marked by low IgG levels. This condition typically resolves after 6 months of age. Option B: DiGeorge syndrome results from a deletion of chromosome 22q11, leading to loss of T cell-mediated immunity. Its characteristic features can be remembered by the mnemonic CATCH-22: Cardiac abnormalities, abnormal facies, thymic aplasia, cleft palate, and hypocalcemia. The absence of the thymus in this condition causes recurrent infections. Option D: Alpha-1 antitrypsin (α1AT) deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by protein misfolding that impairs the secretion of α1 antitrypsin into the serum. This condition affects the liver and the lungs. Pearl PM0536: Primary immunodeficiency disorders

questions.question:
13. A 45-year-old man with midline neck swelling presented with odynophagia and dyspnea. The swelling showed cells with variations in size and morphology. Amyloid deposit was also seen. The swelling was positive for IHC markers TTF-1, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. What is the diagnosis?

IHC - Immunohistochemistry
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario, along with biopsy showing amyloid deposits and positivity for TTF1, synaptophysin, and chromogranin, is suggestive of medullary carcinoma of the thyroid. Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid arises from the parafollicular C cells. Histopathology shows polygonal to spindle-shaped cells forming nests, trabeculae, or follicles. Amyloid deposits, derived from altered calcitonin molecules, are present in the stroma. Calcitonin can be readily demonstrated in tumor cells and the stroma by immunohistochemistry. Features of medullary carcinoma of the thyroid include: * Painful neck mass with cervical lymphadenopathy * Dysphagia, dysphonia, or dyspnea if there is local invasion * Diarrhea due to increased intestinal motility (VIP secretion) * Cushingoid habitus due to ectopic ACTH production * Blood-borne metastases Diagnosis is established by careful family history, physical examination, elevated calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels, and fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the mass. Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid can be associated with RET gene (chromosome 10) mutations in cases of MEN-2A and MEN-2B syndromes.  The following image shows the histopathological slide of medullary carcinoma of the thyroid:

Other options: Option A: Papillary thyroid carcinoma shows papillae lined by cells with overlapping nuclei and Orphan Annie eye nuclei. Psammoma bodies, a form of dystrophic calcification, are its microscopic hallmark.

Option C: Follicular carcinoma of the thyroid is characterized histologically by uniform cells forming small follicles containing colloid, resembling a normal thyroid gland, or sheets of cells without colloid.

questions.question:
14. A young patient presented with PND, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. However, the patient succumbed to her illness. On autopsy, the lungs showed hemosiderin-laden macrophages. In which of the following can it occur except:

PND - Paroxysmal Nocturnal Dyspnea
questions.explanation:
The above clinical case describes heart failure cells, which are intra-alveolar hemosiderin-laden macrophages that indicate chronic passive congestion of the lung leading to pulmonary edema. These cells are not seen in protein-losing enteropathy. In chronic pulmonary congestion, red blood cells leak from the engorged alveolar capillaries into the alveoli, where they are phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages. Within these macrophages, hemoglobin is broken down, leading to the accumulation of brown hemosiderin granules in the cytoplasm. Because of their strong association with pulmonary congestion in congestive heart failure (CHF), these macrophages are called heart failure cells. The following image shows heart failure cells:

Protein-losing enteropathy causes excessive protein loss, leading to reduced intravascular oncotic pressure. This results in fluid shifting into the extravascular spaces, producing ascites, pleural effusion, or pericardial effusion. Occurrence of pulmonary edema is uncommon, and therefore it is not associated with heart failure cells.  Other options: Option A: Right heart failure most commonly develops as a consequence of left heart failure, where ↑ Left Ventricular End-Diastolic Pressure (LVEDP) → ↑ Left Atrial Pressure (LAP) → ↑ Pulmonary Venous Pressure. This venous congestion results in pulmonary edema and the appearance of heart failure cells. Option C and D: Pulmonary venous obstruction and volume overload can both produce chronic passive congestion of the lungs, resulting in pulmonary edema and the presence of heart failure cells.

questions.explanation:
The given pedigree chart is indicative of the Mitochondrial pattern of inheritance, and Kearns-Sayre syndrome is an example of mitochondrial inheritance. Mitochondrial inheritance: * Inherited exclusively from the affected mother (ovum), as an individual’s mitochondrial genome is entirely derived from the mother because sperm contain few mitochondria, which are typically shed upon fertilization. * Both male and female children born to an affected mother will inherit the disease, while an affected father cannot transmit it, and the mother passes it on to all her offspring. 80% of mitochondrial DNA codes for mitochondrial RNA, and therefore most mitochondrial DNA mutations lead to functional problems, which may be manifested as muscle disorders. Kearns–Sayre syndrome (KSS) is characterized by progressive external ophthalmoplegia (PEO), pigmentary retinopathy, and cardiac conduction defects, most often heart block. The disease typically presents before the age of 20 years and may be associated with cerebellar ataxia, progressive myopathy, cognitive decline, and elevated CSF protein levels. A distinctive feature of KSS is white matter disease related to cerebral folate deficiency. It is usually a sporadic disorder caused by mitochondrial DNA deletions. questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question:
1. Identify the true statement regarding free radicals :

1. Lipid peroxidation of membrane lipids 
2. Produced by neutrophils and involved in the respiratory burst
3. Superoxide dismutase inactivates free radicals 
4. Occurs in fibrinoid necrosis
questions.explanation:
1, 2, and 3 are the correct statements. Free radicals can cause peroxidation of lipids within plasma and organellar membranes, in the presence of O2. Oxidative damage begins when the double bonds in unsaturated fatty acids of membrane lipids are attacked by O2-derived free radicals, particularly by OH. The lipid–free radical interactions yield peroxides, which are themselves unstable and reactive, initiating an autocatalytic chain reaction known as propagation that can result in extensive membrane damage. Reactive oxygen species are produced by the rapid assembly and activation of NADPH oxidase, which oxidises reduced NADPH and, in the process, reduces oxygen to superoxide anion. This oxidative reaction is triggered by activating signals accompanying phagocytosis in neutrophils and is called the respiratory burst. Superoxide dismutase inactivates free radicals and acts as an antioxidant by converting hydrogen peroxide to oxygen.

questions.question:
5. A patient suffers from diabetic kidney disease. Which of the following is not a typical glomerular lesion seen?

GBM - Glomerular Basement Membrane
questions.explanation:
Armani-Ebstein lesion is not a typical glomerular lesion seen in diabetic nephropathy. Armani-Ebstein lesions are characterised by vacuolization and PAS-positive glycogen accumulation within the cytoplasm of tubular epithelial cells that are seen only in severe cases of diabetic nephropathy. Loss of podocytes, Mesangial expansion, and Diffuse thickening of GBM are typical glomerular lesions seen in diabetic nephropathy. The most important glomerular lesions are capillary basement membrane thickening, diffuse mesangial sclerosis, and nodular glomerulosclerosis. Thickening of the GBM occurs in almost all cases of diabetic nephropathy and is best appreciated by electron microscopy. These progressive changes are usually accompanied by mesangial widening and thickening of the tubular basement membranes. Diffuse Mesangial Sclerosis consists of a diffuse increase in mesangial matrix. The matrix depositions are PAS-positive. As the disease progresses, the mesangial matrix deposits may take on a nodular appearance. Alterations in the GBM lead to disruption in the filtration barrier and loss of podocytes. Nodular Glomerulosclerosis, also known as intercapillary glomerulosclerosis or Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease, showing nodules of pink hyaline material in regions of glomerular capillary loops in the glomerulus, is a classical finding. The nodular lesions are frequently accompanied by prominent accumulations of hyaline material in capillary loops, known as fibrin caps or adherent to Bowman capsules, known as capsular drops.  The image below shows Armani-Ebstein lesions (glycogen vacuoles in the tubules).

questions.question: 6. A patient underwent a bone marrow transplant without HLA matching. In which of the following disorders does transplant rejection not occur?
questions.explanation:
Transplant rejection does not occur in Bare lymphocyte syndrome. In a patient with bare lymphocyte disease, graft vs host reaction does not occur due to MHC class II deficiency on the lymphocytes. Bare lymphocyte disease occurs due to mutations in transcription factors required for class II MHC gene expression. This results in the lack of class II MHC molecules, leading to the impaired development of CD4+ T cells. As these CD4+ T cells are required for both cellular immunity and for assisting B cells, class II MHC deficiency results in a combined immunodeficiency. Other options: Option A: Jobs Syndrome occurs due to inherited defects in Th17 responses, leading to chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and bacterial infections of the skin. Option B: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome is an X-linked disease characterised by thrombocytopenia, eczema, and a marked vulnerability to recurrent infection, resulting in early death. Option D: Chediak-Higashi Syndrome is an autosomal recessive condition characterised by defective fusion of phagosomes and lysosomes, resulting in defective phagocyte function and increased susceptibility to infections. questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: 7. Which is the most commonly inherited bleeding disorder?
questions.explanation:
Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the most commonly inherited bleeding disorder. VWD is due to abnormal von Willebrand factor (VWF). VWF is an adhesive protein that promotes the adhesion of platelets to subendothelial collagen and stabilises factor VIII. Von Willebrand disease is mostly inherited as an autosomal dominant trait (rarely autosomal recessive). The types of disease include quantitatively deficient vWF (type 1 and type 3) or qualitatively abnormal vWF (type 2). The majority have type 1 disease.  Other options: Option A: Haemophilia A is the most common hereditary disease associated with life-threatening bleeding. Option B: Factor V deficiency is a cause of a rare bleeding disorder, known as parahemophilia or Owren disease. Option D: DIC is an acute, subacute, or chronic thrombohemorrhagic disorder characterised by the excessive activation of coagulation and formation of thrombi in the microvasculature.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: 9. Identify the carcinoma most commonly associated with the following finding.
questions.explanation:
The given image shows lytic lesions in the skull. Follicular thyroid cancer is most commonly associated with it. Follicular thyroid cancer spreads hematogenously to bone, lungs, liver, and other parts of the body. Hence, it can lead to lytic lesions in the skull. Other options: Option A: Hurthle cell thyroid cancer is a variant of Follicular thyroid cancer, but Follicular thyroid cancer has a greater chance of leading to lytic lesions in the skull. Option B: Papillary thyroid cancer leads to lymphatic metastasis and doesn't spread to bones hematogenously. Option D: Thyroid Lymphoma can lead to lymphatic metastasis and doesn't spread to bones hematogenously. Pearl PM2122: Follicular thyroid malignancy It is more common in iodine-deficient areas. It is associated with p53, PTEN, PAX/PPAR-gamma, RAS, miRNA (miR-197 and miR-346). It commonly presents as solitary thyroid nodules and the mean age of presentation is 50 years. It can also occur in long-standing cases of multinodular goitre. FNAC is unable to distinguish between benign and malignant follicular lesions as malignancy is defined by capsular and vascular invasion. Hence, Trucut biopsy is required to confirm malignancy. Histological findings: * Encapsulated * Uniform microfollicles or sheets of cells devoid of colloid * Capsular and vascular invasion indicates malignancy * Tumour thrombus within middle thyroid/ jugular veins may be seen at the time of surgery Vascular (hematogenous) dissemination is common, with metastases to bone, lungs, liver, and elsewhere. The prognosis depends largely on the extent of invasion and stage at presentation. Serum thyroglobulin levels are used for monitoring tumour recurrence, as they are undetectable after complete treatment. Pearl PM2118: Papillary thyroid carcinoma Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid carcinoma. It is most common in iodine sufficient areas, children and in those exposed to ionizing radiation.  The mean age of presentation is 3rd-4th decade and is more common in women than men (2:1). Dysphagia, dysphonia and dyspnea are associated with local invasion. It usually presents as a cold nodule on the scan. Histological findings include: * Branching papillae  * Follicles with the fibrovascular stalk * Psammoma bodies * Nuclear changes-  * Optically clear - Ground glass or Orphan Annie eye nuclei * Pseudo-inclusions * Nuclear grooves. Lymph node metastasis is common. Lateral aberrant thyroid denotes a cervical lymph node invaded by papillary carcinoma. The most common sites of metastasis : lung > liver > bone > brain. It has an excellent prognosis, with a 10-year survival rate in excess of 95%.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: 12. A child presents with petechiae and ecchymosis. His platelet count is 10,000/mm³, and bone marrow is normal with increased megakaryocytes. What is the next best initial step in management?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of a child presenting with petechiae and ecchymosis, a platelet count of 10,000/mm³, and a normal bone marrow with increased megakaryocytes suggests a diagnosis of Acute Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP). The next best initial step in management in this case is IVIG. Acute Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura is characterised by immune-mediated destruction of platelets. It usually occurs in childhood with equal frequency in both males and females. Symptoms appear 1 to 2 weeks after a self-limited viral illness, which appears to trigger the development of autoantibodies through uncertain mechanisms. An increased number of megakaryocytes can be seen in the marrow.  It is characterised by bleeding into the skin and mucosal surfaces. Pinpoint haemorrhages (petechiae) are especially prominent in the dependent areas where the capillary pressure is higher. Petechiae can become confluent, leading to ecchymoses. Often, there is a history of easy bruising, nosebleeds, gingival bleeding, and haemorrhages into soft tissues from minor trauma.  Acute ITP is self-limiting and usually resolves spontaneously within 6 months. Glucocorticoids are given only if the thrombocytopenia is severe.

questions.question: 13. For a 65-year-old female with an adnexal mass, CT was done, which showed ascites. What are the true statements regarding the given specimen? 1. Sex-cord stromal tumour 2. Call-Exner bodies 3. Inhibin positive 4. CA-125 level raised
questions.explanation:
The given clinical vignette of a female with an adnexal mass, CT indicating ascites, histopathology showing call-exner bodies and the gross image are suggestive of granulosa cell tumour, an estrogen-secreting ovarian tumour. Granulosa cell tumours are ovarian sex-cord stromal tumours made up of cells closely resembling the granulosa cells of the ovarian follicle. The majority of the time, it is seen in post-menopausal women. These tumours are usually unilateral. Hormonally active tumours have a yellow colouration due to intracellular lipids that can be seen on their cut surfaces. On histopathology, Call-Exner bodies are seen, which are small, distinctive, glandlike structures filled with an acidophilic material that resemble immature follicles. The serum and tissue inhibin levels are elevated. Granulosa cell tumours sometimes secrete large amounts of estrogen, and they may behave like low-grade malignancies. Functionally active granulosa cell tumours in prepubertal girls may produce precocious sexual development. In adult women, they may be associated with proliferative breast disease, endometrial hyperplasia, and endometrial carcinoma. Androgens may be produced sometimes by granulosa cell tumours which cause virilization of the patient. All granulosa cell tumours are potentially malignant. The most common mutations are found in the FOXL2 gene.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: 14. Inflammation associated with caspase-1 is seen in which of the following types of cell death?
questions.explanation:
Inflammation associated with caspase-1 is seen in Pyroptosis. Pyroptosis is a form of programmed cell death that is different from apoptosis and necrosis. It is involved in the clearance of necrotic and microbe-infected cells. It occurs in the following sequence: * Activation of the inflammasome complex * Activation of caspase-1 * Generation of IL-1 - results in fever, inflammation, leukocyte recruitment Cytoplasmic innate immune receptors recognize microbial products that entered the infected cells and activate the multiprotein complex called the inflammasome. Inflammasome activates caspase 1 and helps in the release of the biologically activated forms of IL-1. IL-1 is a mediator of inflammation, including leukocyte recruitment and fever. Along with caspase 1, caspases 4 and 5 also induce cell death. Pyroptosis differs from apoptosis by the following features: * There is cellular swelling * There is loss of cell membrane integrity * It is associated with inflammation * Caspases 1, 4, and 5 are involved Other options: Option A: Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent, distinct pathway of cell death induced by lipid peroxidation. The widespread peroxidation disrupts membrane function, which leads to the loss of plasma membrane permeability and results in cell death resembling necrosis.  Option B: Apoptosis: The intrinsic mitochondrial and extrinsic death receptor-initiated pathways converge to activate a caspase cascade that mediates the final phase of apoptosis. The intrinsic pathway activates caspase 9, whereas the extrinsic pathway activates caspases 8 and 10. These caspases then activate caspase 3 and caspase 6. Activated caspases cause DNA degradation and nuclear fragmentation. Option C: Necroptosis, as the name suggests, has features similar to necrosis and apoptosis. Like necrosis, it is characterised by loss of ATP, cellular and organelle swelling, the release of lysosomal enzymes, and rupture of the plasma membrane. However, like apoptosis, this is programmed cell death. Ligation of TNFR1 initiates necroptosis. Necroptosis involves two kinases called receptor-interacting protein kinase 1 and 3 (RIPK1 and RIPK3). This is a caspase-independent programmed cell death.

questions.question: 15. Which of the following strains of HPV are more commonly responsible for cervical cancer?
questions.explanation:
Human papillomavirus (HPV) types 16 and 18 are considered high-risk types that are commonly implicated in cervical cancer. HPV 16 and 18 can also lead to vulvar cancer. Condyloma acuminata (venereal warts) is commonly caused by HPV types 6 and 11. However, rarely can HPV 16 and 18 cause it, too.  The E6 protein of high-risk types binds to the p53 gene, while the E7 protein inactivates the pRb gene. p53 and pRb are tumour suppressor genes that, when inactivated, result in uncontrolled cell proliferation. The presence of koilocytes is a histopathological marker of the virus. These cells have a perinuclear halo in the cytoplasm, and these cells disappear when dysplasia advances.  The image below depicts koilocytes.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following is not an intermediate filament?
questions.explanation:
Tubulin is a part of microtubules and is not an intermediate filament.

There are three major classes of cytoskeletal proteins: microfilaments, intermediate filaments, and microtubules.

1. Actin microfilaments:

These fibrils formed from the globular protein actin (G-actin) noncovalently polymerize into long filaments (F-actin) that intertwine to form double-stranded helices.

2. Intermediate filaments:

These rope-like intermediate filament fibers are found predominantly in a polymerized form within cells and do not possess the quality of active reorganization like actin and microtubules. They are responsible for cellular tensile strength, which allows the cells to bear mechanical stress.

Type of intermediate filament Description
Lamin A, B, and C These proteins are localized in the nuclear lamina of all cells. Mutations in lamin proteins are associated with certain disorders such as familial partial lipodystrophy type 2, Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome, and familial dilated cardiomyopathy.
Vimentin These are mainly found in mesenchymal cells (fibroblasts, endothelium).
Desmin Present in sarcomeres in muscle cells.
Neurofilament These are found in neuronal axons, imparting strength and rigidity.
Glial fibrillary acidic protein Present in glial cells around neurons.
Cytokeratins

These proteins are the most diverse among IFs and constitute type I (acidic) and type II (basic) IF proteins.

There are at least 30 isoforms of this protein divided into two groups: Epithelial keratins (found in epithelial cells) and trichocytic keratins (found in hair-keratin).

3. Microtubules:

These are formed by non-covalent polymerization of a dimer of two globular proteins, alpha-tubulin, and beta-tubulin. The microtubules in most cells extend outward from a microtubule-organizing center (MTOC), in which the minus ends of microtubules are anchored.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which test evaluates the extrinsic pathway?
questions.explanation:
Prothrombin time (PT) evaluates the extrinsic pathway of coagulation.

PT measures the clotting time of plasma in the presence of an optimal concentration of tissue extract (thromboplastin). This indicates the overall efficiency of the extrinsic clotting system.

Causes of prolonged PT:

  • Administration of oral anticoagulant drugs - vitamin K antagonists
  • Liver disease - obstructive jaundice
  • Vitamin K deficiency
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation
  • Previously undiagnosed factor VII, X, V or prothrombin deficiency or defect (rare)

Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) measures the clotting time of plasma after the activation of contact factors and the addition of phospholipid and CaCl2, but without added tissue thromboplastin. It indicates the overall efficiency of the intrinsic pathway.

Causes of prolonged APTT:

  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation
  • Liver disease
  • Massive transfusion with plasma-depleted red blood cells
  • Administration of or contamination with heparin or other anticoagulants
  • A circulating anticoagulant (inhibitor)
  • Deficiency of a coagulation factor other than factor VII
  • Intake of oral anticoagulant drugs
  • Vitamin K deficiency

questions.question: A 58-year-old man died 24 hours after the onset of substernal chest pain radiating to the left arm. On autopsy, an atheromatous plaque was seen obstructing the left anterior descending artery. Which type of calcification is most likely to be seen in this condition?

Atheromatous plaques are associated with dystrophic calcification. This is seen in the presence of normal calcium levels in the serum.

The deposition of calcium in dead or dying tissues is called dystrophic calcification. Although it occurs in the presence of normal serum calcium, it can be worsened by hypercalcemia.

Dystrophic calcification is seen in areas of necrosis of any type. Some examples include atheromas of advanced atherosclerosis and areas of caseous necrosis in tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Hepcidin inhibits iron transfer from the enterocyte to the plasma by binding to ________
questions.explanation:
Hepcidin inhibits iron transfer from the enterocyte to plasma by binding to ferroportin.

Hepcidin is released by the liver in response to increases in intrahepatic iron levels. It inhibits iron transfer from the enterocyte to plasma by binding to ferroportin and causing it to be endocytosed and degraded. As a result, iron becomes trapped within duodenal cells in the form of mucosal ferritin and is lost as these cells are sloughed.



Note: In hereditary hemochromatosis, there will be impaired hepcidin synthesis resulting in increased iron absorption.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A CKD patient had to undergo dialysis and his Hb was 5.2gm/dL. So two blood transfusions were to be given. The first bag was completed in 2 hours. The second was started and in the midway, he developed shortness of breath and hypertension. Vitals were BP - 180/120 mmHg and pulse rate - 110/min. What is the cause?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO). 

TACO is caused by rapid or excess transfusion of red cell preparations or plasma products. This condition is characterized by:

  • Dyspnea with O2% <90 at room air
  • Bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray
  • Systolic hypertension
  • Elevation of brain natriuretic peptide, 1.5 times that of pre-transfusion levels

questions.question: If DNA is damaged in the cell cycle, which gene causes cell cycle arrest?

In conditions where there is mutation in p53 gene, the cells with damaged DNA continue to replicate and thus may undergo neoplastic transformation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following is not a hemostatic agent?
questions.explanation:
Boric acid is not a hemostatic agent. 
 
Topical hemostatic agents used in practice include:
  • Hemostatic field dressings
  • Surgical hemostatic agents

1. The hemostatic field dressings are the granular and gauze-based agents which are used to facilitate coagulation and hemostasis. The active ingredients used in various hemostatic field dressings are kaolin, mineral zeolite, and chitosan.

 
Mechanism of action
Advantage
Disadvantage
Kaolin
Cation based activation of the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade
It is non-granular compound. Hence, it does not leave any residue upon removal of the dressing
Clots may be disrupted upon removal. It is less effective in functional or dilutional coagulopathies.
Mineral zeolite
Adsorbs the water, thereby increasing the concentration of the clotting factors, platelets, RBCs.
It is available in two forms:
 
Granular zeolite is effective for pouring into low-flow wounds.
 
The mesh-embedded product is useful in high flow wounds.
The chemical reaction which causes adsorption of water is an exothermic reaction. This causes local tissue damage. The granules may be difficult to be removed.
Chetosan
Poly-N-acetylglucosamine is commonly known as chitin. The deacetylated form of chitin is called chitosan. It has mucoadhesive properties which causes the dressing to adhere to the tissues. It induces vasospasm and attracts RBCs and platelets to the site of bleeding.
It has antimicrobial properties. It can be easily applied and has a long shelf-life.
As the dressing material adheres to the tissues, it may cause disruption of the clots upon removal.

 

2. The surgical hemostatic agents are further divided into the following groups based on the nature of the agent:

 
  • Caustic agents: They act by causing local tissue destruction, which leads to protein coagulation and precipitation. This further leads to thrombus formation and sealing of the small blood vessels. The agents include Monsel solution (a20% ferric nitrate solution), silver nitrate, and aluminum chloride.
 
  • Biological physical agents: They act by promoting platelet activation and formation of three-dimensional matrix for the formation of clots. These agents are used in several operations including neurosurgical, orthopedic, thoracic, abdominal, and vascular procedures. The agents include gelatin, oxidized cellulose, and microfibrillar collagen.
 
  • Physiologic agents: These agents activate a specific step of the coagulation cascade and promotes the clot formation. These agents include thrombin and fibrin glue/sealant.
 
  • Combination or polymer agents: These agents include several different combinations of the above agents and various synthetic hemostatic agents. Examples include gelatin-thrombin agent, polyethylene glycol hydrogel, and glutaraldehyde cross-linked albumin.

questions.explanation:
An inflammatory response is not seen in apoptosis. In this process, the cell membrane remains intact. Hence, there is no leakage of cell contents and no surrounding inflammation.
 
On the other hand, other forms of cell death including necrosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis involve the disintegration of the cell membrane. This causes the cell contents to leak out of the cell leading to an acute inflammatory response.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: An affected male does not have affected children but an affected female always has affected children. Type of inheritance?
questions.explanation:
In mitochondrial inheritance, if the mother is affected and the father is normal, then all their children (both male and female) will be affected. However, children born to an affected father and a normal mother will not be affected.
 
The mitochondrial inheritance pattern is as shown in the image below:


The unique feature of mitochondrial inheritance is maternal inheritance, as the disease is transmitted through the affected mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which is derived from the maternal mitochondria.
 
The ovum contains several mitochondria, while the spermatozoa has very few mitochondria if present. Hence, the mitochondrial DNA of the zygote is entirely derived from the ovum.
 
Therefore, affected mother transmits the disease to all the offsprings (both male and female), and only the daughters of the affected mother, will further transmit the disease.
 
Characteristic features of mitochondrial inheritance:
  • The mitochondrial DNA encodes enzymes required for oxidative phosphorylation. Therefore, organs that are most dependent on the oxidative phosphorylation are the ones most affected in diseases due to mutations in mtDNA. These organs include central nervous system, skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, liver, and kidneys.
  • There are several thousands of copies of mtDNA in each mitochondria, of which only a few copies are affected in case of mutation. Therefore, a diseased individual possesses copies of both wild type mtDNA and mutant mtDNA in each mitochondria  This phenomenon is called heteroplasmy. 
  • The disease manifests if a minimum number of copies of mutant mtDNA are present in the mitochondria that can lead to oxidative dysfunction, called the threshold effect. In most cases, this threshold effect is reached in the organs as mentioned above.
  • Also, during a cell division, the wild and mutant copies of the mtDNA are unequally distributed among the daughter cells. As a result, the expression of the disease varies even among different cells of an organ.

questions.question: True about anaphylactoid reaction are all except:
questions.explanation:
Anaphylactoid reactions are those reactions that are similar to the anaphylactic reactions but are not IgE mediated. These reactions are caused by direct degranulation of the mast cells or basophils, which causes the release of mediators.

Unlike the classic anaphylaxis which occurs on re-exposure to the allergen, the anaphylactoid reaction can occur even on the first exposure. The most common agents that can cause an anaphylactoid reaction include NSAIDs and radiocontrast media.

In 2014, World Allergy Organisation has introduced two new terms:

  • Immunologic anaphylaxis - It includes anaphylactic reactions mediated by IgE, IgG (in animals), and immune complex/ complement-mediated reactions.
  • Non-immunologic anaphylaxis (previously called anaphylactoid reaction) - It includes reactions caused by agents which cause massive degranulation of mast cells or basophils in the absence of immunoglobulin.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Hepcidin inhibits iron transfer from the enterocyte to the plasma by binding to _____
questions.explanation:
Hepcidin inhibits iron transfer from the enterocytes into the plasma by binding to ferroportin, which is an iron efflux channel in the enterocyte.

Iron metabolism is regulated by hepcidin, a protein and acute phase reactant produced by the liver. It binds to ferroportin and degrades it. This inhibits the transfer of iron from the enterocyte to the plasma via ferroportin. As a result, iron becomes trapped within the duodenal cells (enterocytes) in the form of mucosal ferritin and is lost in feces when these cells are shed off.

Transcription of hepcidin is increased by the following factors:

  • Increased levels of iron
  • Inflammatory cytokines

Transcription of hepcidin is decreased by the following factors:

  • Iron deficiency
  • Hypoxia
  • Ineffective erythropoiesis

Hepcidin is encoded by the HAMP gene and its mutations are associated with hereditary hemochromatosis.

questions.explanation:
The image shows a bone marrow biopsy needle. Thrombocytopenia is not in itself a contraindication for bone marrow biopsy. However, a platelet count >20,000 is ensured for safety purposes.

Indications of bone marrow biopsy:

  • Evaluation of unexplained anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, pancytopenia
  • Evaluation of polycythemia, thrombocytosis, leukocytosis
  • Diagnosis and staging of lymphoma or solid tumors
  • Diagnosis and evaluation of plasma cell disorders and leukemias
  • Evaluation of suspected infiltrative and storage diseases
  • Evaluation of fever of unknown origin, suspected mycobacterial, fungal, or parasitic infections, or granulomatous diseases

Contraindications of bone marrow biopsy:

  • Severe hemophilia
  • Severe disseminated intravascular coagulopathy
  • Severe bleeding disorders

Procedure for bone marrow biopsy:

Prone or lateral position is chosen for the procedure. Posterior superior iliac spine is identified. After disinfection and local anaesthesia, the patient is asked to inhale slowly through the nose and exhale slowly through the mouth to relieve anxiety .The needle is inserted and rotated on its axis.

On reaching the desired depth, the stylet is removed and needle is advanced. The needle is rotated in the opposite direction to loosen the specimen. It is then withdrawn using the same rotational movement.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Choose the correct statement regarding the telomerase theory of aging.
options: Telomere stability is associated with aging
Abnormal telomerase activation is associated with aging
Decreased telomere length is associated with aging
Increased telomere length is associated with aging
questions.correct_answer: Decreased telomere length is associated with aging
questions.explanation:
A decreased telomere length is associated with aging.

Telomeres are short TG-rich repeated sequences of DNA present at the ends of linear eukaryotic chromosomes. Telomeres do not code for any proteins. They are important for ensuring the complete replication of chromosome ends and for protecting the ends from fusion and degradation.

Normally, with every cell division, there is some shortening of telomeres at the ends of chromosomes. Once the telomeres are shortened beyond a certain point, it may cause cell-cycle arrest or apoptosis. This is called replicative senescence.

Telomerase is the enzyme that prevents the shortening of telomeres. It is a specialized RNA-protein complex that uses its own RNA as a template for adding nucleotides to the ends of chromosomes.

This enzyme is usually present in germ cells but is absent in most somatic cells. Therefore most of the somatic cells age, their telomeres become shorter and they exit the cell cycle, resulting in an inability to generate new cells to replace damaged cells. Abnormal telomerase reactivation in somatic cells leads to evasion of senescence and apoptosis. It enables the cells to divide several times than usual.

In stem cells and cancer cells, telomerase is usually reactivated and telomere length is stabilized, allowing the cells to proliferate indefinitely.





@Neet_pg_bot

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A child presents with recurrent chest infections and abdominal pain. There is a history of 1 blood transfusion in the past. On examination, he had icterus and mild splenomegaly. Electrophoresis shows increased HbA2, HbF, and S spike. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario with electrophoresis showing increased HbA2, HbF, and S spike is suggestive of sickle cell disease. 

Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the point mutation in the β-globin gene which results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This causes the production of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS).

Factors that predispose to sickling are infection, dehydration, and acidosis.

The clinical features of sickle cell disease are due to the tendency of HbS molecules to stack into polymers when deoxygenated. The features are:

  • Moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice.
  • Painful bone crisis- hand-foot syndrome or dactylitis of the bones of hands and feet.
  • Acute chest syndrome typically presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and pulmonary infiltrates.
  • Hyposthenuria- inability to concentrate urine.
  • Aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia.
  • Spleen
    • In children- splenic sequestration crises occur which results in splenomegaly due to red pulp congestion.
    • Adolescence or early adulthood- autosplenectomy occurs due to splenic infarction, fibrosis, and progressive shrinkage.
    • Increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms like pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenza septicemia, but can be reduced by vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics.
  • Other clinical features- priapism, leg ulcers, stroke, retinopathy, pigment gallstones, and growth retardation.

The diagnosis is suggested by the clinical findings, the presence of irreversibly sickled red cells on peripheral smear, and hemoglobin electrophoresis showing increased levels of HbA2, HbF, and S spike. The changes in the skull resemble a crewcut in radiographic studies as a result of compensatory erythroid hyperplasia.

The image given below shows the sickling of RBCs in sickle cell disease.



The image given below shows Howell-Jolly bodies seen in asplenia.



Note: The sickle cell trait protects against falciparum malaria in certain African populations.

Other options:

Option A: Beta-thalassemia is an autosomal codominant disorder, caused by mutations in alpha or beta globin that reduce hemoglobin synthesis. Peripheral smear shows microcytic, hypochromic cells with anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, target cells, and basophilic stippling. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows increased HbF and HbA2.

Option B: HbC disease is caused by mutation in the beta-globin chain in which glutamate is replaced by lysine in the sixth position of the beta-globin chain. Patients usually present with very mild anemia and microcytosis. Peripheral smear shows hexagonal HbC crystals. Hemoglobin electrophoresis shows increased HbC levels.

Option D: Acute coronary syndrome is very rare in children and may be associated with Kawasaki disease. Children with Kawasaki disease present with fever, conjunctival ingestion, strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, and hand and foot changes. They are treated with intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Why do neoplastic cells utilize Warburg metabolism?
options: It decreases glucose utilisation by neoplastic cells
It forms metabolic intermediates which are needed for cell growth and multiplication
It provides more energy in the form of increased ATP production
It prevents apoptosis and makes the cancer cells immortal
questions.correct_answer: It forms metabolic intermediates which are needed for cell growth and multiplication
questions.explanation:
Neoplastic cells utilize Warburg metabolism for the generation of metabolic intermediates, which are needed for cell growth and multiplication.

The Warburg Effect is a phenomenon in which there is an increase in the rate of glucose uptake and conversion into lactate(fermentation), even in the presence of oxygen. Cancer cells derive energy mainly from glycolysis. 

Cancer cells utilize glycolysis (2 ATP) over mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (36 ATP) for glucose metabolism, even though the latter produces more ATP. It is because pure oxidative phosphorylation produces abundant ATP, but also burns glucose to CO2 and H2O, leaving no carbon moieties suitable for use as building blocks for lipids or proteins.

For this reason, rapidly growing cells, by undergoing glycolysis, produce carbon moieties that are needed for growth and cellular maintenance.

The image given below shows the comparison of glucose metabolism in normal cells versus cancer cells.



As a result of decreased ATP production, the main metabolic function of mitochondria in growing cells is not to generate ATP, but to carry
out reactions that generate cellular building blocks. For example, lipid biosynthesis.

Warburg effect is produced by growth factor receptors downstream signalling pathways. These include receptor tyrosine kinase/PI3K/AKT and MYC.

Clinically, cancer cells exhibiting the Warburg effect show a property of glucose hunger. This is used to visualize them via positron emission tomography (PET) scanning.






@Neet_pg_bot

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: An elderly patient presents with anemia and hemoglobinuria. Investigations reveal increased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). The peripheral smear image is given below. Which of the following physical examination findings can support the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The above scenario with anemia, increased LDH, and hemoglobinuria along with peripheral smear showing schistocytes are suggestive of macroangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA). The presence of a mechanical second heart sound can support the diagnosis. 

Macroangiopathic hemolytic anemia is a type of hemolytic anemia that results from trauma to red cells by artificial mechanical cardiac valves that produce turbulent blood flow and pressure gradients that cause hemolysis from shear forces. This traumatic damage leads to intravascular hemolysis and the appearance of red cell fragments (schistocytes), burr cells, helmet cells, and triangle cells in blood smears.

The given below peripheral smear shows schistocytes and helmet cells.



Laboratory findings in hemolytic anemia resulting from trauma to red cells:

  • Hemoglobin- decreased
  • Reticulocytes- increased
  • Platelets- normal
  • Unconjugated bilirubin- increased
  • Lactate dehydrogenase- increased
  • Haptoglobin- decreased
  • Hemoglobinuria due to intravascular hemolysis

Treatment is conservative. But, if more than mild anemia develops, reintervention to correct regurgitation may be required.

Option A: Splenomegaly is seen in various disorders of white and red cells. But splenomegaly in intravascular hemolysis is less likely.

Option B: Frontal bossing is seen in thalassemia due to expansion of hematopoietically active marrow. An X-ray of the skull shows a 'crewcut' appearance. Peripheral smear in thalassemia shows microcytic hypochromic cells with anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, and target cells.

Option D: Goiter is usually associated with iron deficiency anemia. A peripheral smear shows microcytic hypochromic cells.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: All of the following statements are true regarding neutrophil extracellular trapping (NET) except that
options: It is detected in blood during sepsis.
It is produced in response to bacterial infection.
It is chromatin with antibacterial enzymes.
questions.explanation:
Mitochondrial DNA is not seen in neutrophil extracellular traps (NET).

Neutrophilic extracellular traps are networks of extracellular fibers that provide a high concentration of antimicrobial substances at the site of infection and prevent the spread of the microbes by trapping them in the fibrils.

Neutrophilic extracellular traps (NET) are the meshwork of nuclear chromatin of neutrophils. The loss of nuclei leads to the death of the neutrophils. They concentrate antimicrobial peptides and enzymes to fight against bacteria and fungus (not viruses). They are detected in the blood during sepsis. They are produced by neutrophils in response to:

  • Infectious pathogens: mainly bacteria and fungi
  • Inflammatory mediators: chemokines, cytokines (mainly interferons), complement proteins, and reactive oxygen species (ROS)

Note: The nuclear chromatin in the NETs, which includes histones and associated DNA, has been postulated to be a source of nuclear antigens in systemic autoimmune diseases, particularly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A patient underwent cystoscopy, which showed multiple yellow-white plaques in the trigone of the bladder. The histopathology image is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The cystoscopy findings of multiple yellow-white plaques in the trigone of the bladder and histopathology image showing Michaelis–Gutmann bodies are consistent with the diagnosis of malakoplakia.

Malakoplakia is a rare inflammatory reaction seen in chronic cystitis. It is caused due to acquired defects in phagocyte function, chronic bacterial infection by Escherichia coli or Proteus species, and immunosuppression (renal transplant patients).

The term malakoplakia means soft plaques. Grossly, malakoplakia appears as soft, yellow, slightly raised mucosal plaques. 

Microscopically, they are composed of large, foamy macrophages mixed with occasional multinucleate giant cells and lymphocytes. The macrophages in malakoplakia have abundant granular cytoplasm due to phagosomes stuffed with undigested bacterial products and intracellular deposition of calcium and iron within enlarged lysosomes form laminated basophilic concretions. These are known as Michaelis–Gutmann bodies, pathognomonic of malakoplakia (shown below).



 

The image given below shows the Von Kossa stain demonstrating calcium and iron-containing Michaelis-Gutman bodies (MG bodies) in malakoplakia.



 

Note: Xanthogranulomatous cystitis is morphologically and probably pathogenetically similar to malakoplakia, but it lacks Michaelis–Gutmann bodies.

Other options:

Option A: Interstitial cystitis, also known as chronic pelvic pain syndrome, is a disorder of the urinary bladder that presents with urinary tract symptoms of more than six weeks duration of unknown etiology. Grossly, it is associated with chronic mucosal ulcers called Hunner's ulcers. Microscopically, there is a non-specific increase in mast cells in the submucosa. Biopsy should be done in all cases to rule out carcinoma in situ.

The cystoscopy image shows Hunner's ulcer, seen in interstitial cystitis.



 

Option C: Polypoid cystitis is an inflammatory lesion resulting from irritation of the bladder mucosa, most commonly due to indwelling catheters. The urothelium is thrown into broad bulbous polypoid projections due to marked submucosal edema. They must be differentiated from papillary urothelial carcinoma.

The given image below shows polypoid cystitis showing broad polypoid growth, prominent blood vessels, and metaplastic urothelium in H&E stain.



 

Option D: Acute cystitis is characterized by an inflammation of the urinary bladder following infection, most commonly by Escherichia coli, Proteus, Klebsiella, and Enterobacter. It is more commonly seen in women due to the short urethra. Microscopically, there is hyperemia and neutrophilic infiltration of the mucosa.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following measures are associated with an increased life span?
options: Moderate or regular exercise for 30 min
Pharmacological intervention with proton pump inhibitors
questions.explanation:
Decreasing calorie intake by 30 percent will increase lifespan.

Caloric restriction reduces both the degree of oxidative damage and the associated decline in function. It decreases the steady-state concentrations of products of oxidative damage to proteins, DNA, and lipids. This is due to decreased production of mitochondrial superoxide anion and hydrogen peroxide and increased antioxidant production. Overall, caloric restriction depresses the rate of energy metabolism.

Caloric restriction increases longevity both by reducing the signaling intensity of the insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) pathway and by increasing sirtuins (NAD-dependent protein deacetylases).

The attenuation of IGF-1 signaling leads to lower rates of cell growth and metabolism that reduces cellular damage. A similar effect is produced by rapamycin. An increase in sirtuins (particularly sirtuin-6) promotes the expression of several genes whose products increase longevity by activating DNA repair enzymes through deacylation.

Caloric restriction delays the onset of age-associated diseases such as cancer (including lymphomas and breast and prostate cancers), nephropathy, and cataracts. The onset of diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and the development of autoimmune diseases is also decreased by caloric restriction.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A 56-year-old man was diagnosed with COVID-19 and was put on mechanical ventilation. He passed away after a week. What is the likely post-mortem change seen in the lungs?
options: Thick layer of fibrin lining the alveoli
Pulmonary artery hypertrophy with increased resistance
questions.correct_answer: Thick layer of fibrin lining the alveoli
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario of a patient with COVID-19 pneumonia on mechanical ventilation is suggestive of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). A thick layer of fibrin or waxy hyaline membranes lining the alveolar walls are characteristic of ARDS.

COVID-19 is a respiratory disease caused by SARS-CoV-2. These are enveloped positive-sense RNA viruses. The spread of SARS-CoV-2 is believed to be primarily via respiratory droplets, direct contact, airborne, and fomites.

The major complication in patients with severe COVID-19 is ARDS requiring oxygen therapy and mechanical ventilation. ARDS is a clinical syndrome characterized by acute onset, severe dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and pulmonary infiltrates leading to respiratory failure.

Etiological factors can be divided into direct and indirect causes of lung injury as follows:

Direct lung injury Indirect lung injury
Pneumonia Sepsis
Aspiration of gastric contents Transfusions
Near drowning Drug overdose
Toxic inhalational injury Multiple transfusions
Pulmonary contusion Pancreatitis
COVID-19 Severe trauma like burns, flail chest, head trauma, multiple bone fractures

Damage to the endothelial and alveolar epithelial cells, with inflammation, is the key initiating event and the basis of lung damage. Neutrophils play a significant role in tissue injury in this condition.

There are three stages in the development of ARDS:

  1. Exudative phase- occurs for the first 7 days of the illness. This is associated with damage to alveolar-capillary endothelial cells and type I pneumocytes. This results in a breach in the tight alveolar barrier. The release of proinflammatory cytokines leads to the recruitment of neutrophils and the development of a hyaline membrane in the alveoli.
  2. Proliferative phase- occurs from day 7-21. Recovery from mechanical ventilation is seen in most patients.
  3. Fibrotic phase- is associated with increased mortality. Extensive alveolar duct and interstitial fibrosis are seen.

The image given below shows hyaline membrane formation in the alveolar walls seen in ARDS.



The chest X-ray features in ARDS usually develop 12-24 hours after initial lung insult as a result of proteinaceous interstitial edema. Within one week, a hyaline membrane occurs due to type 1 pneumocyte damage. There are diffuse bilateral coalescent opacities consistent with pulmonary edema. 

The image given below shows chest x-ray findings seen in ARDS.



Berlin's definition of ARDS predicts increased mortality. It considers the following parameters:

  1. Chest X-ray showing bilateral opacities
  2. Respiratory failure within 1 week of alveolar insult
  3. Decreased PaO2/FiO2 ratio to less than 300
  4. Symptoms of respiratory failure are not due to heart failure/fluid overload

Diagnosis of COVID-19 is done by nucleic acid amplification testing of respiratory tract secretions by nasopharyngeal swab. It is associated with elevated inflammatory markers, such as interleukin 6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor, ferritin, C-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, and D-dimer.

Chest CT may be more sensitive than radiographs, but CT should be used principally for medical management of respiratory disease, not as a primary diagnostic tool for COVID-19.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A female patient presented with fatigue. Routine complete blood count analysis showed hemoglobin of 9 g/dL, MCV 60fL, and RBC count of 5.2 million. A peripheral smear showed microcytic hypochromic anemia. Which of the following is the next best investigation for this patient?
questions.explanation:
The next best investigation for this patient would be determining the HbA2 levels, as the history of reduced hemoglobin, reduced MCV (microcytic anemia) and normal to high RBC count is suggestive of thalassemia.

The MCV count divided by the RBC count is called the Mentzer index, which is lower than 13 in thalassemia due to the normal to high RBC count in the denominator. In iron deficiency anemia, it is higher than 13 as the MCV and the RBC count both are reduced.

Alpha- and beta-thalassemia are inherited disorders in which there is reduced production of alpha-globin or beta-globin chains, respectively. This leads to precipitation of the excess (unpaired) chains, interfering with red blood cell (RBC) production and survival.

Clinical features in thalassemia include anemia, jaundice, skeletal deformities including facial deformities, changes in body habitus, growth impairment, and hepatosplenomegaly. Due to frequent blood transfusions, iron overload is also seen. 

Peripheral smear is likely to show microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells, teardrop cells, and some coarse basophilic stippling in certain cases.

The image given below shows peripheral smear findings in thalassemia.



An X-ray of the skull shows a crewcut appearance due to expansion of hematopoetically active marrow.

Thalassemia is usually managed by blood transfusions every 2-4 weeks and chelation therapy with deferoxamine, deferasirox, and deferiprone for iron chelation. Splenectomy is indicated when the transfusion requirement to maintain ideal hemoglobin increases. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is the only known curative treatment for thalassemia.

Other options:

Option A: Serum ferritin level is used to diagnose iron-deficiency anemia (IDA). They are usually low in IDA.

Option C: Serum folate level is used to diagnose macrocytic anemia due to a deficiency of folic acid.

Option D: Serum homocysteine levels are increased in vitamin B12–deficient macrocytic anemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A 56-year-old man presents with dragging pain in the abdomen. On examination, there is massive splenomegaly. Peripheral smear shows leukocytosis with increased myelocytes, metamyelocytes and basophils. Which of the following translocation is seen in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario of massive splenomegaly and peripheral smear shows leukocytosis with increased myelocytes, metamyelocytes and basophils are suggestive of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). A translocation between t(9;22) is seen in this condition. 

CML is a myeloproliferative neoplasm. It is caused due to BCR (on chromosome 22) - ABL (on chromosome 9) fusion gene translocation mutation. It results in the formation of the Philadelphia chromosome which is of CML.

The image given below shows Philadelphia chromosome showing reciprocal (9;22)(q34;q11) translocation seen in CML.



The resulting BCR-ABL translocation results in the activation of tyrosine kinase that signals pro-growth and pro-survival pathways like RAS and JAK/STAT pathways resulting in the proliferation of hematopoietic stem cells.

Patients typically present with a dragging sensation abdomen due to splenomegaly or splenic infarct, fatigue, malaise, and weight loss.

On peripheral smear there is leukocytosis with leukocyte count, often exceeding 100,000 cells/mm3 (neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils), blasts are usually less than 10% of the circulating cells, the platelet count is usually increased.

The image below shows peripheral smear findings of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) with neutrophils, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and band cells.



Bone marrow is hypercellular due to increased numbers of maturing granulocytic precursors with sea-blue histiocytes (macrophages with wrinkled, green-blue cytoplasm).

Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) or polymerase chain reaction(PCR) to detect the BCR-ABL gene. Leucocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score is decreased in cases of CML.

Sokal scoring is used in assessing the prognosis of this patient. The prognosis of CML can be assessed based on:

  • Age
  • Spleen size
  • Platelet count
  • Percentage of blast cells in the blood

FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors for the treatment of CML are imatinib, nilotinib, dasatinib, bosutinib, and ponatinib.

 Complications, if left untreated:

  • Accelerated phase- increased anemia, thrombocytopenia, and basophilia
  • A blast crisis- may transform into acute leukemia (AML/ALL)

Other options:

Options B and D: t(8;14) and t(8;22) are seen in Burkitt lymphoma. It is associated with increased MYC levels. All endemic cases of Burkitt lymphoma are caused by the Ebstein-Barr virus. Microscopy shows a characteristic starry sky pattern.

The image given below shows a starry sky pattern seen in Burkitt lymphoma.



Option C: t(15;17) is seen in acute promyelocytic leukemia. It is characterized by promyelocytes with Auer rods on bone marrow aspirate. All-trans-retinoic acid is used for the treatment.

The image given below shows bone marrow findings in acute promyelocytic leukemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following disorders is caused due to abnormal folding of proteins?
questions.explanation:
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is caused due to abnormal folding of proteins.

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is a prion disease that causes higher cortical function deficits. This infection can be acquired by corneal transplantation, contaminated electroencephalogram (EEG) electrode implantation, dura mater grafts, and contaminated human growth hormone (hGH) preparations.

Symptoms are almost always rapidly progressive, and the clinical presentation includes the following:

  • Myoclonus
  • Higher cortical deficits
  • Psychiatric manifestations - depression, psychosis, and visual hallucinations
  • Profound dementia - memory loss, impaired judgment, intellectual decline
  • Visual impairment or cerebellar gait and coordination deficits in a few patients
  • Nonspecific prodromal symptoms - fatigue, sleep disturbance, weight, loss, headache, anxiety, vertigo, malaise, and ill-defined pain 
  • Extrapyramidal dysfunction - rigidity, masklike facies, choreoathetoid movements;
  • Seizures
  • Hypoesthesia
  • Supranuclear gaze palsy, optic atrophy

Patients commonly present with myoclonus and dementia. EEG shows characteristic periodic electrical bursts. MRI shows increased intensity in the basal ganglia and cortical ribboning (ribbon-like signal hyperintensity of cerebral cortical gyri). On light microscopy, the pathologic hallmarks of CJD are spongiform degeneration and astrocytic gliosis.

 



Other options:

Option C: Nephritic syndrome classically presents with tea- or cola-colored urine (hematuria), edema, hypertension, and oliguria.

Conditions which present as glomerulonephritis:

  • Postinfectious glomerulonephritis
  • IgA nephropathy (Option D)
  • Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
  • Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP) nephritis
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) nephritis
  • Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
  • Goodpasture syndrome (Option C)
  • Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS)
 

Option D: Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the point mutation in the β-globin gene, which results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This causes the production of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS). Factors that predispose to sickling are infection, dehydration, and acidosis. Clinical features are moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice and painful bone crisis. The aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia. In children, splenic sequestration crises occur which results in splenomegaly due to red pulp congestion.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A 65-year-old male patient with chronic fatigue and lymphadenopathy presents to the outpatient department. His peripheral smear shows the presence of smudge cells. Which of the following additional investigations will you do to arrive at a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
An elderly patient with chronic fatigue and lymphadenopathy, and a peripheral smear showing the presence of smudge cells suggest a diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Immunophenotyping using flow cytometry is the investigation done to arrive at the diagnosis. The classical immunophenotypic feature of CLL is CD 19+, CD20+, CD 23+, CD5+.

Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) is a peripheral B-cell neoplasm usually affecting adults, more commonly men. Patients are often asymptomatic at diagnosis. When symptomatic, it presents non specifically with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are present in most symptomatic patients. 

The chromosomal defects in CLL include:

  • Deletion of 13q (commonest and has a good prognosis)
  • Deletion of 11q
  • Trisomy 12q
  • Deletion of 17p (poor prognosis)

The peripheral blood smear in cases of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) contains small round lymphocytes having condensed chromatin and scant cytoplasm. Some of these cells may get disrupted while preparing the smears, producing smudge cells. An absolute lymphocyte count of >5000/mm3 is required for diagnosis. Hypogammaglobulinemia is commonly seen, making the patient susceptible to infections. A few patients may develop hemolytic anemia or thrombocytopenia due to autoantibodies made by non-neoplastic B cells.

On lymph node biopsy: Lymph nodes are composed of small lymphocytes admixed with larger activated lymphocytes. The large lymphocytes contain mitotically active cells and gather in loose aggregates referred to as proliferation centers. These proliferation centers are pathognomic to CLL when present.

Expectant management is the treatment of choice for asymptomatic patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The gold standard for therapy is a combination of fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab.

Richter’s syndrome is a complication of CLL in which there is a transformation to an aggressive lymphoma, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL).

The image shows small round lymphocytes and smudge cells seen in CLL.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about blood products?
options: Platelets is stored between 20°C to 24°C with a shelf life of 5 days.
Cryoprecipitate is stored at -20°C with a shelf life of 6 months
Packed red cells stored with adenine, glucose, mannitol and saline is stored between -5°C to -15°C with a shelf life of 5 weeks
Fresh frozen plasma is stored between -5°C to -15°C with a shelf life of 2 years
questions.correct_answer: Platelets is stored between 20°C to 24°C with a shelf life of 5 days.
questions.explanation:
The statement that is true about blood products is platelets can be stored between 20°C to 24°C with a shelf life of 5 days.

Platelet concentrates can be stored for up to 5 days at +20°C to +24°C, with agitation. It is used in thrombocytopenia, platelet function defects, disseminated intravascular coagulation, during massive blood transfusion to prevent dilutional thrombocytopenia, and in bone marrow failure. Agitation during storage is necessary to maintain their viability and function. This is because platelets are stored at room temperature, where they continue to metabolize glucose and produce lactate. Agitation helps to maintain a uniform distribution of platelets, prevent their clumping together, and facilitate gas exchange.

Fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate are generally stored at a temperature of –30 °C. They are thawed at temperatures between +30 °C and +37 °C in the blood bank before issue and transported to the ward at ambient temperature. They must be used immediately and should never be refrozen.

Whole blood and packed red cells are always stored at +2 °C to +6 °C and transported between +2 °C and +10 °C. Packed red cells stored with SAGM (sodium, adenine, glucose, and mannitol as components) provide a shelf-life of up to 42 days.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A patient with lytic lesions on the skull is suspected of a diagnosis of Langerhan cell histiocytosis. Which of the following is a characteristic finding on electron microscopy?
questions.explanation:
The presence of Birbeck granules in the cytoplasm is a characteristic finding of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) on electron microscopy.

Birbeck granules have a dilated terminal end producing a tennis racket–like appearance. It contains the protein langerin (CD207). It is seen on electron microscopy.

The image below shows Birbeck granules on electron microscopy seen in LCH.



 

Histopathologically, Langerhans cells have a single large nucleus with a characteristic folded or grooved nucleus (coffee-bean appearance) with small inconspicuous nucleoli. Birbeck granules are seen in the cytoplasm. The tumor cells specifically express HLA-DR, S-100, and CD1a and langerin (CD207) markers.

The image below shows histopathological image of Langerhan cells with folded nuclei.



 

Langerhans cell histiocytosis occurs due to the proliferation of a special type of immature dendritic cells, called Langerhans cells. Their normal function is to present antigens. The most common mutation is BRAFV600E gain-of-function mutation.

It is characterized by single or multiple osteolytic bone lesions and can also infiltrate nearly every organ, like the skin (of the scalp), lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, or the central nervous system. 

LCH can present as the following clinical entities:

  • Multifocal multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (Letterer-Siwe disease)
  • Unifocal and multifocal unisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma)- The combination of bone defects, diabetes insipidus, and exophthalmos is called the Hand-Schüller-Christian triad.
  • Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis

The below image shows lytic lesion of skull seen in LCH.
